The child can also keep the runner's output pipes open, delaying failure reporting. Start the scenario in a dedicated process group, forward signals and terminate the whole group before releasing the gate, and add a wrapped-scenario failure test.

threads.body: An override such as `OTEL_CONFORMANCE_OBI_BINARY=./obi` becomes `Path('obi')`, losing the leading `./`. It passes the later `is_file()` check, but `obi_command()` passes the bare name to `Popen` or `sudo`, which searches PATH instead of using that file. This can fail despite a valid override or launch a different installed OBI binary; resolve the override to an absolute path before returning it.

When we aren't root, `obi` is the `sudo -n` wrapper, so on timeout `obi.kill()` SIGKILLs `sudo`. `sudo` can't relay SIGKILL, so the root OBI process keeps running with its probes attached and keeps exporting.

The same thing happens whenever the launcher itself is SIGKILLed: the runner's `subprocess.run(timeout=...)`, or `_kill_tree` in `otel-http-drive` after its shutdown grace period. `_stop` never runs. On CI the VM goes away, but on a dev machine OBI lingers until reboot and can instrument the next run's processes.

Could OBI's lifetime be tied to something the launcher holds? For example, a small root-side wrapper (`sudo -n sh -c '...'`) that starts OBI and kills it when its stdin pipe from the launcher reaches EOF. That pipe closes no matter how the launcher dies. Using `sudo -n kill`/`pkill` on the per-run config path would at least fix the timeout path.
